newsitem.title: CANADA: Crestar Energy sees higher '97 cash flow.
newsitem.headline: Crestar Energy sees higher '97 cash flow.

text.p: Crestar Energy Inc chief executive Barry Jackson, serving notice his firm was on the acquisition trail, said on Wednesday he expected cash flow this year to beat 1996 results and earnings to be about flat.
Jackson told Crestar's annual meeting that the company's cash flow in 1997 was expected to come in at C$277 million to C$289 million or C$5.49 to C$5.76 a share.
The company posted 1996 cash flow of C$263 million or C$5.47 a share.
Earnings for this year were forecast at C$44 million to C$52 million or C$0.92 to C$1.08 a share.
That would be near Crestar's 1996 earnings of C$51.6 million or C$1.07 a share.
Jackson pegged the company's capital spending this year, aimed at drilling 450 operated wells, at between C$300 million and C$330 million.

Financial forecasts were based on an expected average West Texas Intermediate crude oil price of US$19.75 a barrel, which was reduced from an earlier assumption of US$20.50, and gas price of C$1.70 per thousand cubic feet, down from C$1.80, he said.
The estimates also assumed a US$0.72 Canadian dollar.

Jackson told reporters after the meeting that Crestar, which had been widely seen as the No. 2 friendly bidder behind Canadian Occidental Petroleum Ltd in the race for Wascana Energy Inc, was continuing to evaluate potential acquisitions.
The C$2-billion Wascana deal, for which Crestar would have had to offer cash and stock, would be at about the highest price the company would consider, he said.
"That's probably the upper end. As we you start get much larger than that, you run into the problem of us getting swamped by whoever we are doing the transaction with."
He said Crestar was considering a number of acquisition possibilities running the gamut from property deals to corporations that would be similar to its own size.
Crestar currently has a market value including debt and other obligations of about C$1.9 billion.

"Some of the advantages of looking at a transaction that's about the same size as us is that we do have the ability to pool (assets) and that's always attractive from a financial presentation standpoint," he said.
Jackson said the company, after lining up the necessary financing for the Wascana proposal, would have little trouble attracting lenders for a new deal.

"The lending community -- we have a favorable relationship with them so we wouldn't see problems with some cash," he said. "We couldn't do a deal the size of Wascana on a cash basis...there would have to be a significant amount of paper in the deal."
The company's last major acquisition was its C$266 million takeover of Ranchmen's Resources in late 1995.
Without a major acquisition, the company expects to produce about 43,000 barrels of oil and natural gas liquids per day and 347 million cubic feet per day of natural gas this year.
That would be up from 37,000 barrels per day of liquids and 319 million cubic feet per day of gas in 1996.
